title: The new notification timing gets a higher open rate overall — switch everyone to it?

scenario.role: You're the lifecycle-marketing analyst at Dayspring
scenario.situation: A contextual policy rolled a new push-notification send time out more aggressively to weekday-active users before ramping weekend-only users. Looking at overall open rate across all notifications, Sana, the lifecycle lead, sees the new timing beating the old one and wants to switch every user to the new send time this week.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: "Across all notifications, the new send time gets a higher open rate than the old one. Let's switch everyone to it this week."
scenario.question: Did the new timing actually open better within the weekday-active cohort and within the weekend-only cohort, or does the overall number just reflect how the rollout allocated traffic? Split the comparison by cohort before switching everyone.

columns.name: user_cohort
columns.description: weekday_active or weekend_only — the user's usage pattern

columns.name: arm
columns.description: new_timing or old_timing — which send time this notification used (allocated unevenly by cohort — weekday_active got new_timing far more often than weekend_only did)

columns.name: opened
columns.description: 1 if the notification was opened — the reward

guidingQuestions: Reproduce Sana's number: mean opened for arm == new_timing versus old_timing, pooled across all notifications. How big is the win?
What share of notifications got new_timing within weekday_active versus within weekend_only? Was the new timing allocated evenly across cohorts?
Now compute the new_timing vs. old_timing open-rate gap SEPARATELY within weekday_active and within weekend_only. Does the new timing actually win in either cohort?
Compare weekday_active's overall open rate to weekend_only's, regardless of timing. Which cohort opens more, and how does that interact with which timing got more traffic in which cohort?
If the new timing loses within every cohort but wins pooled, what is the pooled number actually measuring?
suggestedApproach: Reproduce the pooled gap: mean(opened) for new_timing minus old_timing across all notifications.
Check the share of new_timing within weekday_active notifications and within weekend_only notifications separately — look for an uneven allocation.
Split the open-rate comparison by cohort: compute the new_timing vs. old_timing gap within weekday_active only, then within weekend_only only.
Compare baseline open rates by cohort to see whether one cohort opens substantially more than the other regardless of timing.
Explain how an uneven traffic split across a higher- and lower-opening cohort can flip the pooled sign relative to every individual cohort — classic Simpson's paradox.

notebook.intro: Five steps: reproduce the pooled win, check how the sends were allocated, then compare the timings on equal ground.

cells.title: Reproduce the pooled gap
cells.explain: Start with the claim itself — new_timing's open rate minus old_timing's, across every notification.
cells.code:
rates = df.groupby("arm")["opened"].mean() * 100
pooled_gap = rates["new_timing"] - rates["old_timing"]
print(f"pooled gap (new_timing - old_timing): {pooled_gap:+.2f} pts")
rates.round(2)
cells.reads: The pooled number favours the new timing. The question is whether the two arms were sent to comparable people.

cells.title: Check how the sends were allocated
cells.explain: Look at what share of each cohort's notifications went to each arm. An even split would make the pooled number trustworthy.
cells.code:
mix = pd.crosstab(df["user_cohort"], df["arm"], normalize="index") * 100
print("share of each arm within each cohort (%)")
mix.round(1)
cells.reads: The allocation leans opposite ways in the two cohorts, so the arms are not facing the same audience.

cells.title: Compare the timings within each cohort
cells.explain: Hold the cohort constant so the allocation cannot do any of the work.
cells.code:
by_cohort = df.groupby(["user_cohort", "arm"])["opened"].mean().unstack() * 100
by_cohort["gap"] = by_cohort["new_timing"] - by_cohort["old_timing"]
by_cohort.round(2)
cells.reads: Check the sign of the gap in each cohort against the pooled gap from cell 1.

cells.title: See which cohort opens more anyway
cells.explain: A mix can only flip a result if the segments differ in the outcome too. Check that here.
cells.code:
baseline = df.groupby("user_cohort")["opened"].mean() * 100
print("open rate by cohort, ignoring the arm (%)")
baseline.round(2)
cells.reads: One cohort opens far more regardless of timing — and it is the cohort the new timing was given most of.

cells.title: Put the two numbers side by side
cells.explain: Re-weight both arms to one common cohort mix and compare again.
cells.code:
within = df.groupby(["user_cohort", "arm"])["opened"].mean().unstack()
weights = df["user_cohort"].value_counts(normalize=True)
adjusted = within.mul(weights, axis=0).sum() * 100
adj_gap = adjusted["new_timing"] - adjusted["old_timing"]
print(f"mix-adjusted gap: {adj_gap:+.2f} pts")
pd.DataFrame({"effect (pts)": [pooled_gap, adj_gap]}, index=["pooled", "mix-adjusted"]).round(2)
cells.reads: Once both arms face the same cohort mix the pooled advantage does not survive. The allocation was the story.

teachingNote.naiveRead: Pooled across all notifications, the new send timing gets a higher open rate than the old one. That reads as a clear win — obviously switch everyone to it.
teachingNote.theTrap: The rollout policy didn't allocate the new timing evenly: weekday-active users got new_timing 72% of the time, while weekend-only users got it only 28% of the time (a weekday-first ramp). Weekday-active users also open notifications far more than weekend-only users regardless of timing. Split the comparison by cohort and the new timing actually LOSES in both: -1.7 points for weekday-active and -4.0 points for weekend-only. But because the new timing's traffic is disproportionately weekday-active (the higher-opening cohort) and the old timing's traffic is disproportionately weekend-only (the lower-opening cohort), the pooled comparison mixes a favorable cohort for the new timing with an unfavorable one for the old timing — and the pooled number flips positive even though the new timing never actually wins anywhere. This is Simpson's paradox, driven here by unequal bandit/rollout allocation rather than a random split.
teachingNote.honestAnswer: Always split a bandit or rollout comparison by the segments traffic was allocated across, especially when the allocation itself wasn't uniform. Here, the honest, cohort-level answer is that the old timing gets a higher open rate for both weekday-active (-1.7 points for new_timing) and weekend-only (-4.0 points for new_timing) users — the pooled +3.8 point 'win' is entirely a traffic-mix artifact of the weekday-first rollout, not a real effect of the new timing. Tell Sana: don't switch everyone to the new timing. If anything, the data argues for keeping the old send time, or investigating why the new timing underperforms in both cohorts before rolling it out anywhere.
howToGetThere: Compute the pooled gap: mean(opened | new_timing) minus mean(opened | old_timing) across all notifications ≈ +3.8 points.
Check new_timing's share by cohort: 72% for weekday_active vs. 28% for weekend_only — a strongly uneven allocation from the rollout policy.
Split the gap by cohort: weekday_active ≈ -1.7 points (old_timing wins), weekend_only ≈ -4.0 points (old_timing wins) — new_timing loses in both cohorts.
Compare cohort baseline open rates: weekday_active opens meaningfully more than weekend_only regardless of timing — the cohort new_timing got more of is simply a higher-opening cohort.
Conclude: the pooled 'win' is a mix-shift artifact of unequal traffic allocation, not a real effect of the new timing — Simpson's paradox.

numbers.label: new_timing share of traffic: weekday_active vs. weekend_only

teachingNote.lesson: A bandit or phased rollout that allocates traffic unevenly across segments — even for reasonable operational reasons, like ramping the most active users first — can produce a pooled result that reverses what's true in every individual segment, the same Simpson's paradox mechanism as any confounded observational comparison. Whenever an arm's traffic share differs across a variable that also affects the outcome, split the comparison by that variable before trusting the pooled number. A policy that loses in every segment cannot be a real winner overall — the pooled 'win' is measuring the traffic mix, not the policy.
